title: The Rashomon Effect or the Downside of Being Smart
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Named for the 1950 Kurosawa film in which four witnesses describe the same murder in contradictory ways, this Field Note argues that intelligent people are especially prone to constructing self-serving narratives that mask confirmation bias. Because smart leaders are skilled storytellers, they can make biased decision-making look rational and objective even to themselves. The recommended countermeasure is deliberately generating a second, independent narrative on the same facts -- often via another leader, colleague, or red team -- and comparing it against one's own account before finalizing a major decision.
points: Smart people are described as especially skilled at constructing self-serving narratives that mask their own biases.
The Rashomon Effect (from the 1950 film) illustrates how people describe the same events in contradictory ways.
Confirmation bias is triggered specifically by the narrative-construction process during major decisions.
The recommended countermeasure is deliberately generating a second, independent narrative on the same facts.
Red teams are said to add the most value when they construct a competing narrative, not just contrary facts.
quotes: Smart people are more prone to let their biases cloud their thinking.
Known as the Rashomon Effect in cinema, it’s named after a 1950 Japanese film in which four witnesses describe a murder in four contradictory ways.
Rather than deny this sense-making and the biases it contains, great decision-makers seek a second narrative on the same facts and information.
By comparing the competing narratives during the decision-making process, the leader is less likely to be blind to their biases or to allow them to operate unchallenged.
The power of a story to shape meaning should never be taken lightly.
